China's Inflection Point Could Be Here 

(First published on Sparta's Market Outlook on 21 August, and point number 8 is already happening, with FOB premiums going up and eroding the cracking margins)

1⃣At least 8 mb of Basrah Medium and Basrah Heavy cargoes have been sold to Rongsheng and some state-owned Chinese refiners for prompt delivery, with Basrah Medium rumoured to be at CFR Dubai + sub 10$/bbl levels.

2⃣This is apparently in reaction to missing out on the eighth ADNOC tender (they probably tried to bid for cheaper cargoes but failed).

3⃣Pre-crisis, from Sparta’s rolling front month arbs, the delivered pricing of Basrah Medium spot cargoes was around $2/bbl lower than Oman cargoes into Far East. With Oman currently landing around Oct Dubai+$19/bbl, the pricing of Basrah Medium at CFR Dubai+$10/bbl sounds reasonable.

4⃣On the Saudi allocations front, the quantity allocated to China is now heard to be 14 mb, just 1-2 VLCCs higher than the last three months of 10-12 mb allocations. Zhenhua was heard to have been allocated as well, signalling the start-up of the 300 kb/d HAPCO refinery is imminent.

5⃣There was also 10 mb of Arab Medium and Arab Heavy crudes heard sold on a rare Saudi Aramco tender to Petrochina, Sinochem, Unipec and Rong Sheng for prompt loading.

6⃣Russian ESPO is heard to be sold out for October loaders, whilst Iranian offers are few and far between for the independent refiners.

7⃣As a result, traders are seeing more active inquiries from both state-owned players and independent refiners.

 8⃣This should translate to higher achievable FOB premiums, given cracking margins are still in double digits in the Asian markets even with eye-watering freight rates.

9⃣Product exports could start creeping up around October if the crude buying pattern is sustained as well. We will of course need to hear the actual refined product export quotas to confirm.

#oott

Re: the ongoing debate about how much oil is getting through Hormuz and whether a particular WH claim is “True”, so so so much comes down to charity of the claim treatment and tone/framing of the assessment.

For example, a claim of 18 MMbbl over a given day can be an especially charitable clipped 24(ish) hour period—true in a tortured sense while misleading or cherry-picked.

Or a really high non-specific number can be charitably interpreted to mean the full broader middle east (with reroutes) rather than Hormuz, specifically.

Or a claim of 9 MMbpd when, say, only 6-7 MMbpd is confirmable can be both said to be “broadly” or “directionally” correct while at the same time being a “plausible exaggeration”. Or if that pace was only realized weeks after the claim it’s just “early.”

This is all fine! But given both the obvious fogginess of the data and the acute political undercurrent to the topic, best if folks are specific.

FWIW, I currently see Hormuz petroleum flows (crude + products) in the ballpark of 8 MMbpd**, with some of that representing re-displaced Saudi crude from the Red Sea.

And based on my tracking I have generally judged White House Hormuz transits numbers are directionally correct, plausible, but cherry-picked and often meant to mislead (like Trump’s 18 MMbbl claim).

**Chart below, highest I’ve confirmed thus far (with adjusted Kpler data) is just more than 8 MMbpd, with the current level lower but expected to be revised higher to roughly that same level.

There’s also the fact that the only way they’re managing to get this much oil through is thanks to enormous US military support, massive exporter discounts, ludicrously high insurance, etc.

Been long Copper since 2023. Not naive enough to expect up-only in a straight line, but the macro thesis is still screaming bull.

S&P Global dropped some great charts, so let’s strip away the noise and run through the structural supply:

1) The tier-1 discovery pipeline is in a total desert. Down from 714.8Mt in the ‘90s to a pathetic 8.7Mt over 2020–2025. Mega discoveries are basically extinct.

2) Capex burns are back up past $3B annually on exploration, yet the hit rate is completely cooked—netting a measly 0-2 discoveries a year. Trash ROIC... 

3) Discovery cost per tonne went from ~$10 in the ‘90s to an eye watering $1,000–$2,600+ print today. Not a temporary blip; it’s a secular blowout in finding costs.

4) Gone are the days of unlocking multi tens of million monsters like Collahuasi or Pebble. Today’s wins are 1–2Mt crumbs that don't move the global balance needle.

5) More than half (55%) of cumulative reserves are concentrated in South America, while Africa—such as the DRC—is gradually taking up a larger share. South America has recently slipped into operational and production slumps, and Africa continues to suffer from political instability.

6) Roughly 500Mt of identified reserves have been rotting in prefeasibility purgatory for decades. Permitting hell, eco-lawfare, and zero IRR. Bless the regulators and green grifters for choking.

7) C-suites are terrified of greenfield risk. They’ve completely castrated wildcat budgets to hide inside safe brownfield pit extensions. Structural consequence. Zero chance of hitting a generational tier-1 asset.

8) Copper mining typically takes over 15-20 years from discovery to actual commercial production (operational), the current exploration slump translates directly into a future production cliff. This is an undeniable fact.

9) Megawatt power grids, EV buildouts, and AI data centers are devouring physical units, while the project pipeline is running bone dry. Sure, the demand ceiling floats on the macro tape, but this structural supply paralysis puts a bulletproof concrete floor under the market.

10) Marginal incentive pricing and long term cost floors have nowhere to go but violently up and to the right.

So what's priced into the equities? Large caps are still riding a fat liquidity premium over the mid/small cap complex. Ivanhoe’s lagging for obvious DRC baggage, but look at the implied copper price deck.

In the week to 1 September, the combined managed-money net long across ten major grain and soft commodity futures jumped by 266k contracts to 1.37 million contracts, the highest since records began in 2006 and representing a nominal value of around USD 53 billion.

A hot US jobs report adds another twist to this week’s roller-coaster action across markets. Gold has reversed sharply lower, down 1.9% to USD 4,385, while the dollar and Treasury yields move higher as rising short-end yields once again lift expectations for a 16 September Fed rate hike.

Bottom line: the jobs report was strong across the board. August payrolls beat expectations and prior months were revised higher, while the unemployment rate remained low despite an increase in the participation rate, pointing to continued labour-market resilience even as the workforce expanded. Average hourly earnings were in line with expectations despite an uptick in weekly hours worked.

The main caveat is that these surveys are subject to substantial statistical adjustments, with nonfarm payroll estimates in particular often undergoing sizeable revisions. Still, the initial read is clearly hawkish for the Fed.

Attention now turns to next week’s CPI report (11 September), which could prove decisive for the September decision, particularly following Governor Waller’s comments yesterday highlighting the importance of incoming inflation data.

#Agriculture:  The @UNFAO Food Price Index rose 1.9% in August, a third consecutive monthly gain, while the year-to-date increase remains a moderate 2.5%. All commodity groups recorded higher prices, led by sugar (+11.9% m/m, +7% y/y), dairy (+2.3% m/m, -19% y/y) and grains (+2.2% m/m, +10.9% y/y).

On the sugar surge, the FAO highlighted growing concerns over the 2026/27 global supply outlook. Hot and dry weather has reduced EU sugar beet yield forecasts, while El Niño-related conditions are threatening production across key Asian producers. Lower output in Brazil’s Center-South region and India’s announcement of duty-free raw sugar imports added to the tightening outlook.

International cereal prices also rose across all major grains in August, supported by strong demand, weather-related concerns over US and EU crop yields, robust feed and ethanol demand, and continued uncertainty over Black Sea exports.

Vegetable oils rose just 0.6% in August but remain the biggest contributor to food price gains over the past year, up 17.2%. Higher palm and soy oil prices outweighed weakness in sunflower and rapeseed oils, with palm supported by strong import demand and El Niño-related production concerns in Southeast Asia.
